questions.story: The Nasdaq is in a healthy uptrend. Today it slips 0.3% on volume a bit higher than yesterday. There hasn't been a day like it in weeks.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Log it, one day means little
Sell everything at the open
Short the Nasdaq right away
Ignore it, a 0.3% dip doesn't count
questions.answer: Log it, one day means little
questions.why: Log it and move on. Under IBD's rule it does count: 0.3% down on higher volume clears the 0.2% bar. But IBD says one distribution day here or there won't hurt a healthy uptrend. What IBD warns about is a cluster, five or six in a few weeks. So keep the count going. Until it builds, hold your stocks and let your stops do their job.
questions.lesson_line: One distribution day is noise. Start paying attention when they pile up.

wrong.Sell everything at the open: A few distribution days in an uptrend are no reason to dump your stocks. One is even less.
wrong.Short the Nasdaq right away: One day of selling isn't a trend change.
wrong.Ignore it, a 0.3% dip doesn't count: Under IBD's rule it does. The bar is a drop of 0.2% or more on higher volume.

questions.simple: Write it down and move on, because one distribution day doesn't hurt an uptrend. A cluster does.

deeper.trap: The trap is reacting to the first one. IBD says a random distribution day here or there won't hurt an uptrend, and even a few during a confirmed uptrend aren't reason enough to dump all your stocks. Keep the count and let it build before it changes what you do.

reasons: rests on IBD's rule, which can change

questions.story: In four weeks the S&P 500 has logged six distribution days. Several of your leading stocks are breaking support.
questions.q: Read IBD's way, what's this telling you?
choices: A warning, time to get defensive
Healthy, keep buying breakouts
Meaningless without a recession
A follow-through day is near
questions.answer: A warning, time to get defensive
questions.why: Time to get defensive. Six distribution days in four weeks is the cluster IBD warns about. A cluster alone doesn't stop a rally right away. What makes this one serious is your leaders breaking support. Major tops come with exactly that pair: a flurry of distribution and the leaders cracking. So I lock in profits, cut losers fast, and I'm not hunting for new buys here.
questions.lesson_line: A pile of distribution days plus cracking leaders means get defensive.

wrong.Meaningless without a recession: The market tends to peak well before the economy does.
wrong.A follow-through day is near: A follow-through confirms a new uptrend after a correction. You're at the other end.
wrong.Healthy, keep buying breakouts: A cluster like this warns that the uptrend is weakening.

questions.simple: Get defensive, because six distribution days in four weeks plus weak leaders is the warning sign.

deeper.counter: IBD's own words are hedged. It says a cluster doesn't stop a rally at once, but it's a smart time to get defensive by locking in profits and cutting losses short. It also says major tops are preceded by a flurry of distribution days and severe weakness among the leading stocks. The leaders breaking is what makes this case strong.

reasons: rests on IBD's cluster rule, which can change

questions.q: The market is trending up and distribution days start to cluster. A price drop reliably follows.
questions.why: False. Bulkowski tested it. Clusters within 21 calendar days in a rising trend did not predict a drop. They only worked in a falling trend, heavy volume or light. So treat the count as a caution light, not a forecast. IBD reads a cluster as a time to get defensive, and that's sensible. But your stocks and price make the call, not the count.
questions.lesson_line: A distribution count is a caution light, not a sell signal. Price and your stocks decide.
questions.simple: False, because tests found clusters in a rising market did not predict drops. They only worked in falling markets.

deeper.trap: The trap is the word 'reliably'. IBD reads a cluster as a warning to get defensive, and that is a sensible caution. But Bulkowski's tests say a rising-trend cluster is not a dependable forecast of a drop. Treat the count as a caution light, and let price and your own stocks decide.

questions.q: The market's been bouncing off a low for a few days. What would IBD call a follow-through day?
choices: A strong index gain on higher volume
Strong index drop on higher volume
The first up day after a market low
An index gap up that holds all day
questions.answer: A strong index gain on higher volume
questions.why: A strong index gain on higher volume, a few days into the bounce. The Nasdaq or S&P 500 closes up big from the day before, on more volume than the day before. IBD reads it as the selling likely being over and a new uptrend starting. For me it's a sign to start looking for buys again, a few names at a time, not a reason to go all in. Our Breadth charts have a toggle that marks follow-through days.
questions.lesson_line: A follow-through day says the bounce off the low has real buyers behind it.

wrong.Strong index drop on higher volume: That's a distribution day, the selling side.
wrong.The first up day after a market low: Too early. The follow-through comes on Day 4 or later.
wrong.An index gap up that holds all day: A gap isn't the test. It's a strong close above the prior day on higher volume.

questions.simple: It's a strong index gain on higher volume, a few days after a market low.

reasons: rests on IBD's rule, which IBD can change (read from 2012-2015 republished articles)

questions.story: After a long selloff, the Nasdaq closes at a new low on Tuesday. It closes higher Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, never undercutting that low. Monday it gains 1.8% on higher volume than Friday.
questions.q: What does IBD call Monday?
choices: A follow-through day
A distribution day
Day 1 of a rally attempt
A failed rally attempt
questions.why: A follow-through day. Count it out. Tuesday is the low. Wednesday is the first up close, so that's Day 1 of the rally attempt. Thursday is Day 2, Friday Day 3, Monday Day 4. IBD wants the signal on Day 4 or later. It calls the gain needed a moving target, at least 1% to 1.25% in one version. Volume has to beat the day before. Monday's 1.8% on higher volume clears both. The low never broke, so the attempt stayed alive. Not every one works, so start small.
questions.lesson_line: Count from the first up close after the low. Day 4 or later, a strong gain, more volume.

wrong.A distribution day: Distribution needs the index to fall. It rose.
wrong.Day 1 of a rally attempt: Day 1 was Wednesday, the first up close after the low.
wrong.A failed rally attempt: It fails only if the index undercuts its low. It never did.

questions.simple: Monday is a follow-through day, because it's Day 4 of the rally attempt and the gain came on higher volume.

deeper.trap: Two traps. First, counting the low day itself as Day 1. IBD's Day 1 is the first up day after the low, so Tuesday does not count. Second, treating the signal as an all-clear. IBD says the follow-through isn't perfect, so don't immediately get fully invested. Some follow-throughs fail, and the market falls to new lows.

reasons: IBD's gain threshold is a moving target

questions.q: A follow-through day just fired. IBD's advice is not to go fully invested right away.
questions.why: True. The signal isn't perfect. It says the selling has likely ended, not surely. Some follow-throughs fail and the market goes on to new lows. That's why we ease in. A few positions first, then more as they work. If the follow-through fails, you've lost a little and you're still mostly in cash.
questions.lesson_line: A follow-through day opens the door. It doesn't mean go all in.
questions.simple: True, because the signal isn't perfect and some follow-through days fail.

deeper.counter: A follow-through day can fire and then fail, with the market reversing to new lows. That is why IBD warns against getting fully invested at once.

reasons: statement reworded in wave8 to IBD's own advice; the key is now True

questions.story: A follow-through day fires on a session full of grim headlines. Most people you know are still bearish.
questions.q: Do the headlines change how you read it?
choices: Bad news is normal at a follow-through
Wait for good news to confirm it first
Grim headlines cancel out the signal
It needs a Fed rate cut to count
questions.answer: Bad news is normal at a follow-through
questions.why: No. Bad news is normal at a follow-through. These form when fear is high and most people are still bearish. If you wait for the news to feel good, you'll be late. The signal is the index's price and volume, not that week's headlines. Read the market, not the news.
questions.lesson_line: Follow-throughs show up while the news still looks bad. Read price and volume, not headlines.

wrong.Wait for good news to confirm it first: Headlines are a poor guide to the start of an uptrend. IBD says most investors are still scared when it comes.
wrong.Grim headlines cancel out the signal: IBD says a follow-through doesn't have much to do with the week's headlines.
wrong.It needs a Fed rate cut to count: IBD's test is price and volume. Policy news isn't part of it.

questions.simple: Bad news is normal, because follow-throughs form amid fear and grim headlines, while most investors are scared.

deeper.trap: The trap is waiting for the news to feel safe. IBD says most investors are scared or bearish when a follow-through comes, and that it doesn't have much to do with that week's headlines. StockCharts says these days form amid fear, negative headlines and persistent selling.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass

questions.q: You hear the market is in a rally attempt. In IBD's terms, where are we?
choices: The first bounce off a market low
A confirmed new market uptrend
A rally to a new all-time high
A short squeeze in a single stock
questions.answer: The first bounce off a market low
questions.why: Right off the low. A rally attempt starts when a falling index bottoms and turns up. The first up day is Day 1. Nothing's confirmed yet. If the index undercuts that low, the attempt fails and it starts over. Confirmation comes later, with a follow-through day. Early rallies fail a lot, so use this stretch to build your list, not to load up.
questions.lesson_line: A rally attempt is a question. The follow-through day is the answer.

wrong.A rally to a new all-time high: A rally attempt starts right off a market low, nowhere near a high.
wrong.A confirmed new market uptrend: Confirmation comes later, with a follow-through day.
wrong.A short squeeze in a single stock: A rally attempt is about a major index, not one stock.

questions.simple: A rally attempt is the first bounce after a falling index bottoms and turns higher. Nothing's confirmed yet.

reasons: rests on IBD's rule, which IBD can change (read from 2012-2015 republished articles)

questions.story: The S&P 500 rose 1% today. Yet more of its stocks fell than rose, so its A/D line dropped.
questions.q: How can both be true?
choices: Big caps weigh more in the index
The A/D line has a data error
Volume was too light to count
The A/D line lags the index by a day
questions.answer: Big caps weigh more in the index
questions.why: Big caps weigh more in the index. The S&P 500 is cap-weighted, so the biggest companies move it most. The A/D line gives every stock one vote. A few giants jump, most stocks slip, and you get exactly this: index up 1%, A/D line down. Neither number is wrong. They measure different things. That's why I watch both. When they split like this, the rally is narrower than it looks.
questions.lesson_line: The index weighs by size. The A/D line counts heads. Watch both.

wrong.The A/D line has a data error: Both are right. They just weigh stocks differently.
wrong.Volume was too light to count: Volume doesn't enter the A/D line at all. It counts stocks up versus down.
wrong.The A/D line lags the index by a day: Both use the same day's closes. The gap comes from how each one weighs stocks.

questions.simple: The big companies count most in the index, while the breadth line gives every stock one vote, so the two can disagree.

deeper.example: Picture a day when a few of the largest companies jump and most smaller members slip. The index rises, because those few carry most of the weight. The A/D line falls, because more members declined than advanced. Tom McClellan describes this as buying in a few big caps that the rest of the market is not confirming. He calls any divergence a condition, not a signal.

reasons: fixed before (a distractor replaced by the checker)

questions.story: The market just came out of a correction. The app's market reading, our market filter, flips back to Green, its healthy reading. You hold no stocks yet.
questions.q: How do you start buying again?
choices: A few positions, more as they work
Buy a full book of stocks that same day
Add to your first trade as it rises
Wait for the reading to hold a month
questions.answer: A few positions, more as they work

wrong.Buy a full book of stocks that same day: If the turn is a head fake, every stop hits at once. Start with a few.
wrong.Add to your first trade as it rises: Rebuilding is new positions, not more shares in one trade. Each goes on at full size, once.
wrong.Wait for the reading to hold a month: You start when the reading turns Green. A few positions, not a waiting period.

questions.simple: Start with a few positions, then add more positions only as the first ones work.
questions.why: A few positions, then more as they work. The first Green day after a correction can be a head fake. Buy a full book, it fails, and every stop hits at once. Start with a few of your best setups. If they work, the market's telling you the turn is real, and you add more positions. If they fail, you lost a little and you're still mostly in cash. Each trade goes on at full size, at one price, with one stop. Let the market earn your exposure.
questions.lesson_line: After a correction, ease back in: a few positions first, more only as they work.

deeper.trap: The trap is going all in the day the reading turns Green. Start with a few positions instead, and add more positions only as the first ones work. Don't rebuild by adding shares to one trade: each goes on at full size, at one price, with one stop.

reasons: a rule from the owner's rulebook (F68, A5, B18)

conflicts: IBD's own pages show only the opening lines to non-subscribers (s38 is cited for its open lead only). The distribution-day and follow-through-day rules come from full IBD articles republished on Yahoo Finance (2012-2015, s30-s34). IBD's live rule could not be read, so every question says 'IBD's method' or 'IBD's rule', and all six IBD sources share one publisher name so they never count as two publishers.

Follow-through gain: IBD calls it 'a moving target' (2015: 'at least 1% to 1.25%'; 2012: '1.3% to 1.4% or more'). No question asks for a threshold. q61's 1.8% gain clears both versions, and its key also rests on the day count and the volume test.

Follow-through timing: IBD 2015 says 'Day 4 or thereafter'; IBD 2013 says four or more sessions in, but 'once in a while, they can occur earlier' (with early ones more often short-lived). q61 keys a Day 4 signal only; no question asks whether an earlier day can count.
Distribution-day threshold: 0.2% is in IBD 2014 (s30) and IBD 2015 (s31), and Bulkowski says his test used 'more than 0.2%' to match IBD (s35). q55 keys 0.2 as IBD's rule only.

Distribution days, rule vs test: IBD treats a cluster of five or six in a few weeks as a warning (s30, s31; Bulkowski quotes the same IBD research). Bulkowski's tests (stocks 2005-2010, S&P 500 1950-2010) found clusters in a rising trend did not predict drops and worked only in a falling trend. The file teaches IBD's reading as IBD's (q58) and Bulkowski's finding as his (q57 wrong note, q59, w3).

McClellan Oscillator versions: ChartSchool and Investopedia give the 19-day minus 39-day EMA of net advances; McClellan Financial describes the same pair as EMAs with 10% and 5% smoothing constants; ChartSchool's own oscillator is ratio-adjusted. q38 states its own EMA values and keys only fast minus slow; no question asks for an oscillator level.
McClellan Summation Index level: McClellan Financial says the properly calibrated index is neutral at +1000; ChartSchool's version fluctuates around zero. No question asks about its level.

Breadth thrust: ChartSchool's oscillator thrust runs from below -50 to above +50; Investopedia's is a move of 100 points or more from negative to positive; Martin Zweig's breadth thrust is a different, 10-day measure (not used). q43 and q44 key only the shared idea, a sudden surge of broad buying; q44's -70 to +60 fits both oscillator definitions.

TRIN extremes: ChartSchool's 'above three oversold, below 0.50 overbought' is for the unsmoothed daily NYSE TRIN (its 10-day smoothed example uses 1.20 / 0.80); Investopedia gives 3.00 / 0.50. q53 says 'daily NYSE TRIN' and keys only the direction (oversold), with ChartSchool's advice to trade with the bigger trend.

Up and down volume: Nasdaq's glossary and ChartSchool sort volume by whether the stock closed up or down on the day. Investopedia's 'Upside/Downside Ratio' page sorts it by close versus the day's open. The file uses the Nasdaq / ChartSchool definition and does not cite that page.

Percent of stocks above a moving average: ChartSchool calls 70% / 30% overbought / oversold for the 50-day version and says levels vary; Schwab calls 80% above the 50-day 'solid bullish breadth' and under 10% a hint of an overdone selloff. No question keys a fixed threshold: q33 uses Schwab's own 80% example and q34 keys only 'wait for an upturn'.
